questions.question: Tell me about a time you led a major change initiative.
questions.text: The largest change initiative I have led is the ERP modernization at Kohl & Frisch, where as AI & ERP Integration Lead between 2019 and 2023 I directed the end-to-end move onto Microsoft Dynamics 365, including the legacy IBM AS/400 migration work. I led a 45-person cross-functional team through an 18-month platform migration while keeping 7 distribution centres running on one ERP/WMS/TMS stack. My approach was to sequence the cutover by business function, keep operations leaders inside the decision loop, and run change management as a workstream with its own owner rather than an afterthought. The transformation delivered a 30% reduction in operating costs.

questions.question: Describe a situation where you had to overcome a significant technical challenge.
questions.text: The hardest technical problem I have solved was connecting LLM agents on Azure OpenAI to order processing that ran on the legacy IBM AS/400 and Manhattan DFIO stack at Kohl & Frisch, systems that were never designed to expose structured APIs. I built the integration layer myself: ERP write-back tools with output validation, retrieval tools over the warehouse and supply chain data, and a harness with error recovery so a failed call never left a half-written order. The difficult part was getting agents to handle the exceptions that order clerks resolved by habit, which meant encoding those rules as explicit tool logic and confirmation gates rather than trusting the model to infer them. The result was a 68% reduction in manual order processing time.

questions.question: How do you handle disagreement with a technical decision from leadership?
questions.text: There is no specific leadership dispute documented here, so I will describe how I handle one. My rule is to disagree with evidence rather than opinion: I write down the decision as proposed, the risk I see, the data behind that risk, and an alternative with its cost, then take it to the decision-maker directly instead of airing it in a wider room. During the 18-month ERP migration at Kohl & Frisch, sequencing and scope decisions went through exactly that process, with the 45-person team's dependency and risk picture in front of leadership rather than my preference. If leadership still chooses differently after seeing the evidence, I execute their decision fully and keep measuring, because a decision made with the facts visible is legitimate even when it is not mine.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you made a decision with incomplete information.
questions.text: The decision I would point to is the scope of the tier-1 IT chatbot at Kohl & Frisch: I had to choose which query types the agent would handle before there was any production evidence of how staff would actually use it. The historical ticket data could not tell me that, so rather than wait for a perfect dataset I launched with a narrow, well-understood query set, kept a human escalation path on every response, and instrumented the escalations so the gaps became visible quickly. Each expansion of scope was then based on live traffic rather than assumptions. The principle I apply: decide on the evidence available, make the uncertainty explicit, and build the feedback loop that turns it into evidence.

questions.question: How do you prioritize when you have competing high-priority projects?
questions.text: When I was directing the ERP modernization at Kohl & Frisch and building the AI procurement agent in the same period, both had executive sponsors who considered theirs the top priority. My method is to make the tradeoff explicit rather than absorb it: I map each workstream against business impact, risk of delay, and the dependencies between them, and I put that picture in front of leadership so the sequencing decision is theirs. I then protect the sequence by refusing to let unplanned work in unannounced; new requests go onto the same board and visibly displace something. The migration involved a 45-person team over 18 months, which is long enough that priorities will shift, so the review happened on a regular cadence rather than once at kickoff.
highlights: ERP and procurement agent in parallel

questions.question: Describe a time you influenced without formal authority.
questions.text: Most of the agentic workflow automation I have led at Kohl & Frisch depended on procurement and warehouse operations teams that did not report to me. My approach is to start with one of their own problems, run a small pilot inside their process, and report the result in their units of measure: hours of manual work removed, exceptions resolved, orders that no longer need a human touch. I let the team's own supervisors present the pilot results upward, which turns them into sponsors rather than recipients. That is how the automation of 16 operational processes expanded across functions without a mandate behind it.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you pushed back on a stakeholder's request.
questions.text: A specific stakeholder dispute is not something documented here, so I will describe how I handle the situation. When a request would put an agent into production before its guardrails are ready, I do not simply say no; I lay out the options with their risks: ship as asked with the risk written down, ship a limited rollout with a human escalation path, or delay until validation is complete. On the agent deployments at Kohl & Frisch, where tools have write-back access to ERP records, my position is that confirmation gates and output validation are not negotiable, and I say so before the schedule conversation starts. Once the stakeholder chooses with the risks visible, I own the outcome of that choice.

questions.question: How do you build trust with a new team or organization?
questions.text: I build trust by listening before I propose anything. When I moved into the AI & Agent Systems Lead role at Kohl & Frisch in 2023 my first step was to sit with warehouse operations and IT support staff to learn what they actually needed from AI and which manual steps cost them the most time. Then I picked one visible, well-bounded problem and delivered on it quickly so the team could judge the work rather than the pitch. From there I keep trust by being precise about what an agent can and cannot do yet, and by making every automated action traceable, so no one has to take the system on faith.

questions.question: Describe a time you mentored or developed someone on your team.
questions.text: A specific mentoring relationship is not documented here, so I will describe how I develop people. My method is working sessions on a real problem: with the analysts and engineers on my team at Kohl & Frisch, I take a live warehouse or procurement question, design the prompt and the tool calls together, and have them evaluate the output critically before anything ships. The goal is that they can judge an agent's output independently, since a team that depends on me to validate every result does not scale. I measure my own success as a mentor by how little the team needs me on the next project.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you missed a deadline — what happened and what did you do?
questions.text: A missed deadline is not something documented in my record here, so I will describe how I handle one when it threatens. On the 18-month ERP platform migration at Kohl & Frisch, I protected the schedule with named owners and written definitions of done for every dependency, which is where slips usually show up first. When a date is at risk, my rule is to call it the day I know, with the root cause and a revised plan, rather than hoping to recover quietly; a phased delivery that lands the core function first is usually the honest option. Stakeholders can plan around early bad news, and they cannot plan around a surprise.

questions.question: How do you set expectations when working across multiple teams?
questions.text: Cross-functional programs fail at the handoffs, so I set expectations at the handoff level. On the 18-month ERP migration at Kohl & Frisch, I led a 45-person team spanning IT and operations functions, and every dependency between them got a named owner, a date, and a written definition of done; verbal agreements did not count. Weekly reviews went through that dependency board rather than status slides, so a slipping handoff was visible to everyone it affected. Each team also knew exactly which decisions were theirs and which were escalated, which removed most of the friction before it started.

questions.question: Describe a time you had to deliver bad news to an executive.
questions.text: A specific instance of delivering bad news is not documented here, so I will describe my practice. I brief the executive the same day the problem is confirmed, and I bring four things: what happened, what it means for timeline and cost, the options with their tradeoffs, and my recommendation. On the ERP modernization at Kohl & Frisch, every material risk on the 45-person program went to leadership in that format, which meant nothing reached the executive sponsor late or second-hand. Bad news delivered early is a decision request; bad news delivered late is an apology.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you delivered under a tight timeline with limited resources.
questions.text: The tier-1 IT chatbot at Kohl & Frisch is the clearest example: a small engineering team, a firm launch date, and a user base of 2,400 warehouse staff across 7 distribution centres. I cut scope to the single highest-value use case, tier-1 IT queries, and deferred every other request to a later wave, which was the unpopular decision and the right one. I reused the harness, retrieval tools, and observability hooks already built for other agents instead of standing up new infrastructure, and I kept a human escalation path so a thin launch could not become a bad one. The agent now handles 90% of tier-1 IT queries.

questions.question: Describe a situation where data or analysis changed your mind.
questions.text: I started the WMS AI optimization at Kohl & Frisch assuming pick-path routing was the main lever for pick accuracy. Before building anything, I instrumented the existing pick process on the Manhattan DFIO WMS and let the baseline error data set the order of work, and that baseline did not match my assumption: the errors were concentrated in steps I had not planned to touch first. I rebuilt the roadmap around what the data showed and moved routing to a later phase. Pick accuracy reached 99.7%, which I would not have gotten to by optimizing the step I had planned to optimize.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you aligned multiple teams around a shared goal.
questions.text: At the start of the ERP modernization at Kohl & Frisch, I had a 45-person cross-functional team whose members each measured success differently, and an 18-month migration does not survive that. I opened the program by having each function map its own operational pain points, and the roadmap was built out of that exercise rather than handed down from my office. When people co-author the plan, they defend it in their own budget and staffing conversations, which is the alignment that actually holds. I then kept the shared goal visible through a single dependency board and one set of milestone reviews that every function attended.
highlights: pain points mapped by each function

questions.question: How do you balance technical debt against shipping new features?
questions.text: My rule is that I will accept interface and workflow debt to ship faster, and I will not accept data schema debt or integration debt, because in AI systems a shortcut in the data layer corrupts everything built on top of it. On the agent deployments at Kohl & Frisch, where tools have write-back access to ERP records, that meant reporting features and conveniences could be deferred while input sanitization, output validation, and confirmation gates could not. I keep the deferred items on a visible list with an owner so the debt is a decision, not a surprise. The test I apply to any shortcut: if it fails, is the failure contained to a screen, or does it reach a purchase order?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you took ownership outside your defined role.
questions.text: A specific out-of-role incident is not documented here, so I will describe how I treat ownership. During the intelligent WMS deployment across 7 distribution centres at Kohl & Frisch, the work that threatened the schedule was rarely the AI itself; it was upstream data quality and integration issues that sat with other teams. My practice is to pick up the blocking work myself when I have the capacity and the context, document the fix, and hand it back to the owning team with a pattern they can reuse, rather than waiting for an escalation chain to run its course. Ownership for me is a decision about outcomes, not a reading of the org chart.

questions.question: How do you handle an AI system behaving unexpectedly in production?
questions.text: A specific production incident is not documented here, so I will describe the protocol I run. Step one is containment before diagnosis: the harness halts write-back to the ERP for the affected agent and routes its work to human review, so an unexplained output cannot become an unexplained purchase order. Step two is tracing, which is why every agent call at Kohl & Frisch is logged with its tool calls, retrieved context, and output, so I can find the step that went wrong rather than guessing at the model. Step three is a permanent guard: a validation rule, a tighter authorization scope, or a confirmation gate that would have caught the same class of failure, added before the agent returns to full autonomy.

questions.question: Describe a time you had to shut down or pivot a project you believed in.
questions.text: A project I had to kill is not documented in my record here, so I will describe how I make that call. I set the exit criteria before the build starts: the business metric the system has to move, the cost it has to stay under, and the point by which it must show evidence, so stopping is a comparison against a written threshold rather than an argument with my own attachment to the design. On the AI procurement agent at Kohl & Frisch, that meant tracking purchase cycle time and human overrides against the agreed targets from the first pilot onward. When something I designed does not clear the bar, I say so first, before anyone else has to.

questions.question: How do you approach AI ethics and responsible deployment?
questions.text: Responsible deployment, for me, is an engineering practice rather than a policy document. Every agent I deploy at Kohl & Frisch is threat-modeled for technical failure (hallucination, prompt injection, tool output poisoning) and for human impact, meaning any automated decision that affects a person's work or a supplier's business gets a human confirmation gate rather than silent autonomy. Agents operate under least-privilege scoping, every action is logged and traceable, and staff are told plainly what the system does and does not decide. People use AI they can audit; they work around AI they cannot.

questions.question: How do you approach building an AI team?
questions.text: I hire for domain depth first and AI skill second, because a supply chain analyst who learns to prompt, evaluate, and distrust an LLM output will outperform a strong ML engineer who does not know what a 3PL is. I structure a team around three roles: builders who own the harness and data pipelines, domain adapters who translate the business problem into tools and evaluation criteria, and evaluators who own quality and security. At Kohl & Frisch that mix is what lets a small team serve 2,400 warehouse staff with agents that touch live ERP and WMS data. I also keep everyone on the team building, including me; an AI team that only reviews slide decks loses touch with the failure modes.

questions.question: How do you know when an AI project is actually successful?
questions.text: Model accuracy is the least useful measure of an AI project; it says nothing about whether the business problem is solved. I measure success in three layers: operational (is the process faster or cheaper, in units finance can audit), adoption (are the intended users actually routing work through it), and trust (are escalations and overrides falling over time rather than rising). At Kohl & Frisch the clearest example is the IT support agent, which handles 90% of tier-1 queries; that is an adoption number, and it only holds because staff stopped routing around the system. The $2.4M reduction in operating costs from AI automation is the operational layer, and it was defined before the build, not after.

questions.question: How do you explain complex AI to non-technical stakeholders?
questions.text: I lead with the problem and the number it moves, never with the technology. When I presented the IT support agent to executives at Kohl & Frisch, I did not describe a retrieval-augmented LLM with tool routing; I said warehouse staff would get tier-1 IT questions answered without waiting on a ticket, and I named the share of queries I expected it to take off the help desk. Technical detail comes after the business case is accepted, and only at the depth the listener needs to make a decision. The same discipline applied to the 2,400 staff who would use it: they were told what it does, what it cannot do, and who to call when it is wrong.

questions.question: How do you stay current in the rapidly changing AI landscape?
questions.text: I stay current by reading primary sources and testing on real problems. I follow model and research releases from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and NousResearch directly rather than through summaries, and every framework I am curious about gets tried against a live supply chain task, not a toy dataset; LlamaIndex, AutoGen, and CrewAI are under active evaluation right now alongside LangChain in production. I also run open-source models through OpenCode, my self-hosted OpenAI-compatible server, so I can evaluate a release without waiting on a vendor. The real discipline is knowing what to ignore: the durable concepts are agent harnesses, memory architecture, and security threat models, and not every model release is worth a context switch.

questions.question: Tell me about a failed AI project and what you learned.
questions.text: A failed project is not something documented in my record here, so I will tell you where I expect AI projects to fail and how I build against it. In my experience the model is rarely the point of failure; the data and integration layers are, which is why on the LLM-powered demand-forecasting agents at Kohl & Frisch I put validation gates on the ERP data feeds ahead of inference and a human review step on any recommendation that leaves the expected range before it reaches a purchase decision. I also treat staging results with suspicion until live ERP feeds have run through the same pipeline, because a clean snapshot hides exactly the variance that breaks production. The lesson I carry is to fund the data integration and the observability first and treat the model as the easy part.

questions.question: How do you build AI agents with harnesses and workflows?
questions.text: I start with the harness: the execution loop that owns tool routing, error recovery, and observability hooks before any model reasoning enters the picture. On top of the harness I build domain skills, which at Kohl & Frisch means supply chain data retrieval, ERP write-back with output validation, and warehouse query tools against the Manhattan DFIO WMS. Workflows then compose those skills into plan, act, observe, reflect loops, using ReAct for single-agent tool use and Plan-and-Execute when the task needs a committed sequence of steps. That architecture is what runs the 16 operational processes I have automated end-to-end, and the harness is the reason a failed tool call becomes a retry or a human handoff rather than a bad ERP record.

questions.question: What agent orchestration frameworks have you used?
questions.text: LangChain is what I run in production for tool-routing agents at Kohl & Frisch. I am actively experimenting with LlamaIndex for retrieval-heavy pipelines, AutoGen for multi-agent conversation patterns, and CrewAI for role-based crews, each tested against a real supply chain task before I form an opinion. My honest view is that frameworks speed up prototyping and then abstract away the control production needs, so I pair them with my own harness layer that handles observability, error recovery, and authorization outside the framework's scope. For agents where a bad tool call can raise a real purchase order, that harness layer is not optional.

questions.question: How do you design multi-agent systems and handle inter-agent trust?
questions.text: Multi-agent systems add a trust problem single agents do not have: when one agent delegates to another, the receiving agent has to know the instruction is legitimate and not a prompt injection carried along in the first agent's output. My architecture gives every agent a declared capability scope, validates inter-agent messages against a schema before anything executes, and makes it structurally impossible for an agent to escalate its own privileges or call tools outside its scope. I also treat tool output and retrieved content as untrusted input, so poisoning one agent's context does not hand authority to the next. At Kohl & Frisch this runs as a coordinator agent orchestrating specialised sub-agents across procurement and warehouse operations, and I red-team the delegation paths before any of it reaches production.

questions.question: What is your tech stack for building AI agents?
questions.text: Python is the core, with Azure OpenAI (GPT-4o) and Claude as my primary LLM APIs and Google Gemini in the evaluation mix. LangChain handles tool orchestration in production, wrapped in my own harness layer for observability, error recovery, and authorization. For self-hosted inference I run OpenCode, an OpenAI-compatible server, serving NousResearch Hermes locally or on a VPS; retrieval is RAG with vector search, and quality is tracked with LLM-as-judge evaluation and hallucination rate monitoring. On the Microsoft side, Power Automate, AI Builder, and Copilot Studio cover the workflow integrations that do not need a custom agent. The bar for anything in this stack is that it survives a bad tool call without a human having to intervene.

questions.question: Tell me about your LLM memory research.
questions.text: The core problem I am working on is that most agents are amnesic: every session starts from zero, even when the same supplier has missed the same delivery window repeatedly. My research covers three memory layers: episodic memory, which stores and retrieves past agent interactions and decisions; semantic memory, a knowledge graph of domain facts such as SKUs, supplier data, and SLAs; and working memory, the context window management that long-horizon planning tasks need. I apply these patterns to supply chain agents at Kohl & Frisch that need operational history to make a sound procurement or inventory decision. The goal is agents that accumulate operational judgement over time, not just raw capability.

questions.question: What is your work on agent security?
questions.text: Autonomous agents have an attack surface most security teams have not mapped yet: prompt injection through retrieved content, tool output poisoning, and cross-agent trust escalation. I start with threat modeling, enumerating what an adversarial input could cause the agent to do, and then build the defenses into the harness rather than the prompt: input sanitization before tool calls, output validation before any write-back, privilege containment, and least-privilege action scoping with confirmation gates on destructive operations. I red-team my own agentic systems to find and close attack paths before deployment, because the agents at Kohl & Frisch have write access to ERP records and a successful injection there has a real cost. Security is a property of the harness, not a feature of the model.

questions.question: What is RAG and when would you use it?
questions.text: RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, grounds an LLM's answer in data retrieved at query time instead of whatever it memorised in training. You index source documents into a vector store, retrieve the most relevant chunks for the query, and place them in the prompt before the model answers. I choose RAG over fine-tuning whenever the data changes often (inventory, pricing, supplier records, policies) or when citations and auditability matter, which is every case in pharmaceutical distribution. Fine-tuning is justified for stable behaviour such as output format or domain vocabulary, not for knowledge that moves daily.

questions.question: How do you evaluate and monitor LLM performance in production?
questions.text: Production LLM monitoring tracks latency, token cost, hallucination rate, and user outcome at the same time, and I instrument for all of them. Every inference call is logged with structured fields (model, prompt version, token counts, latency, tool calls, user rating) and fed to a dashboard with alert thresholds on tail latency and cost per query. For quality I use LLM-as-judge scoring against a rubric on every response, hallucination rate monitoring as a tracked metric, and periodic human review of flagged outputs so the judge itself gets audited. The number I care about most on the agents at Kohl & Frisch is the escalation rate, because a falling escalation rate means users are trusting the answers, and that is the only quality signal finance will accept.

questions.question: What is fine-tuning and when should you use it instead of RAG?
questions.text: Fine-tuning locks knowledge into the model's weights at training time, so every data change means a retraining cycle; RAG keeps knowledge in a store you can update without touching the model. For enterprise use that difference decides it: in pharmaceutical distribution, where SKUs, pricing, and supplier data change daily, RAG is the only architecture I would put in production for factual answers. I use fine-tuning selectively for behaviour that rarely changes, such as a consistent output format, domain vocabulary, or tone. The two also combine well: a lightly fine-tuned model for format discipline, with RAG supplying the facts at query time.

questions.question: How do you handle hallucinations in production LLMs?
questions.text: Hallucinations are the cost of probabilistic generation, so the engineering question is whether the system catches them before they reach a decision. My defence is layered: RAG grounding so answers are based on retrievable records, structured output schemas that constrain what the model is allowed to produce, and LLM-as-judge evaluation that scores every production response against a rubric. Anything that fails the judge or falls outside its schema routes to a human rather than to the ERP. I track hallucination rate as a monitored production metric at Kohl & Frisch, and a rising rate triggers a review of the retrieval layer first, because that is where the cause usually is.

questions.question: Explain zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting.
questions.text: Zero-shot is instruction only: you tell the model what to do with no examples. Few-shot adds worked examples of the exact output you want, which is the cheapest quality gain available since it needs no training. Chain-of-thought asks the model to reason step by step before answering, and it helps most on logic, multi-step decisions, and domain analysis where the first instinct is often wrong. On the enterprise agent prompts I maintain at Kohl & Frisch, I combine few-shot examples with chain-of-thought and measure the difference with LLM-as-judge scoring rather than assuming it; the gain is real but task-dependent, which is why I test it.

questions.question: How do you reduce LLM inference latency and cost at scale?
questions.text: Inference cost and latency decide whether a production AI system is sustainable, so I work both at once. I cache frequent query patterns to avoid redundant API calls, route classification and triage tasks to smaller models while reserving GPT-4o or Claude for the reasoning steps that need them, and stream responses so perceived latency improves even when raw speed cannot. For self-hosted workloads I serve open-source models such as NousResearch Hermes through OpenCode, which removes the per-token bill entirely for the right tasks. Every change is measured against cost per query and a quality score from LLM-as-judge evaluation, because a cheaper answer that users escalate is not cheaper.

questions.question: What vector databases have you used and how do you pick one?
questions.text: I pick a vector database by where the product is in its lifecycle, not by its marketing. For a RAG prototype I start with an embedded or in-database option such as ChromaDB or pgvector, which adds no infrastructure and no new bill; a managed service such as Pinecone or Weaviate is justified only when production latency and scale demand it. In pharmaceutical distribution, where retrieval on supplier records and drug SKUs has to be exact, I weight hybrid search (dense plus sparse retrieval) over pure vector similarity because it handles the long-tail queries that embedding search misses. The metric I evaluate on is retrieval precision at k on my own queries, not a benchmark score.

questions.question: What is LoRA and when would you use parameter-efficient fine-tuning?
questions.text: LoRA, Low-Rank Adaptation, is parameter-efficient fine-tuning: instead of updating every weight, it trains small low-rank adapter matrices injected into the attention layers, so a large open-source model such as NousResearch Hermes can be adapted at a fraction of the compute of full fine-tuning. QLoRA goes further by quantising the base model to 4-bit, which brings fine-tuning within reach of a single GPU. I reach for LoRA when I need a model to produce a specific domain output reliably, for example structured field extraction for ERP records, and few-shot prompting alone is not consistent enough. For factual knowledge that changes, I still use RAG; LoRA is for behaviour, not for facts.

questions.question: How do you handle documents that exceed the LLM context window?
questions.text: My default for long documents is retrieval first: chunk the document by semantic boundaries rather than by raw token count, embed and index the chunks, and retrieve only the passages relevant to the query. Dumping an entire compliance document into a large context window invites the lost-in-the-middle problem, where content buried in the centre gets ignored. For documents where sequential reasoning matters, such as contracts, audit trails, and order histories, I use a map-reduce pattern: summarise each chunk independently, then synthesise the summaries with the original passages available for citation. Working memory management is one of my LLM memory research areas, and the same discipline applies to agents on long-horizon supply chain planning tasks.

questions.question: What is your approach to LLM observability and tracing in production?
questions.text: Observability is what separates teams that know their agent is working from teams that hope it is. I instrument every agent call with a structured trace: model ID, prompt version, token counts, latency, each tool call with its arguments and result, and the output score from LLM-as-judge evaluation, all feeding a dashboard with alert thresholds on tail latency, cost per query, and hallucination rate. For agentic workflows I trace the full reasoning chain, every intermediate step and every retry, so when a multi-step workflow fails I can see which step failed and what context it had. These observability hooks are built into my harness at Kohl & Frisch rather than added afterwards, which is the only way they survive the next framework change.

questions.question: What supply chain AI systems have you built?
questions.text: The supply chain AI at Kohl & Frisch is a connected set of agents rather than one system. LLM-powered demand-forecasting agents run on ERP supply chain data and delivered a 13% improvement in forecast accuracy; an AI procurement agent cut purchase cycle time by 33%; and the WMS AI integration on Manhattan DFIO took pick accuracy to 99.7% across 7 distribution centres, with a 15% improvement in warehouse throughput. In my current role I orchestrate these as agentic workflows, with 16 operational processes automated end-to-end and agents serving 2,400 warehouse staff. Together they are the reason AI at Kohl & Frisch is operational infrastructure rather than a pilot program.

questions.question: How have you integrated AI into ERP, WMS, and TMS systems?
questions.text: Integrating AI into ERP, WMS, and TMS systems is a data integration problem before it is an AI problem. At Kohl & Frisch I built the integration layers that turn data from the Manhattan DFIO WMS on IBM AS/400 and from Microsoft Dynamics 365, the ERP platform, into structured inputs that Azure OpenAI agents can reason over, with ERP write-back tools validated before any record changes. The TMS integration feeds transportation data into the same supply chain agents, so forecasting and procurement decisions see carrier and delivery constraints. The ERP transformation reduced operating costs by 30%, and the AI procurement agent layered on it cut purchase cycle time by 33%.

questions.question: How do you measure ROI on AI projects?
questions.text: I agree the ROI definition before the build: the cost of the current manual process, the projected cost with AI, and the delta, in dollars and hours that finance can audit rather than accuracy scores that only engineers can measure. Every AI initiative at Kohl & Frisch was framed that way, which is why the results read as business numbers: a $2.4M reduction in operating costs from AI automation, 90% of tier-1 IT queries handled by the agent, a 68% reduction in manual order processing time, and a 33% reduction in purchase cycle time from the procurement agent. I also track the cost side honestly, including inference spend and the human review time the guardrails require. If a number cannot be tied to a ledger line or a timesheet, it is not an ROI figure.

questions.question: How do I write better prompts for ChatGPT?
questions.text: The biggest single upgrade is giving the model a role, the context, and a constraint: who it is, what you need, and what you do not want. Instead of 'summarise this', write 'You are a senior analyst; summarise this report into a short list of bullet points for a CFO and leave out technical jargon'. Add 'think step by step' for anything involving reasoning, and paste in one example of the output you want when format matters. On the enterprise agent prompts I maintain at Kohl & Frisch, these same principles live in versioned prompt templates, and I measure them with LLM-as-judge scoring rather than trusting that they worked.
